utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Tieger, I asked the witness to be stand by. I would like to ask you, in chief until now, you've taken one hour and 45 minutes. Today we could expect to have approximately four hours. That would make five hours and 45 minutes. The witness was scheduled for six witness. Do you intend to conclude the examination-in-chief today, or... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, two matters: Number one, I had understood that the witness estimate was eight hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's so, then I should immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was our understanding as well, Your Honour. Eight hours has been consistently what we have been given on the schedule, so we agree with Mr. Tieger about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see. I thought that I saw on one of the schedules six hours, but if that's wrong, then I have to withdraw my question at all. If I find any six hours somewhere, I'll draw your attention to that. Yes. The latest schedule says time estimated: Six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can only repeat what I said before. We had been operating on the understanding, as has the Defence -- let me also say notwithstanding that estimate, I think the Court is aware that we have made considerable efforts to bring our direct examinations in well under the time. That's my intention here as well, but I think I need to emphasise that I understood I was operating under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least -- I took it from the list, which says at the bottom "as of the 22nd of June," so since today it's the 23rd of June, I thought this was the most recent information. If you have another --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not -- well, we do have another. It's that we don't have or never have seen any such document as the one that Your Honour is referring to with a later date. So we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have eight hours on the 22nd of June, and we have six hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The last one that we have is dated the 17th of May 2004, Krajisnik order of proof at 24th May to 9th July, and it sets eight hours. And, Your Honour, when I spoke, as we often do, of course, we do talk to each other, when I spoke to Mr. Tieger within the last day or so, and he confirmed and said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep it short. On the basis of the latest information, I thought I should put this question to you. But now it turns out that this information is, for one reason or another, is not correct information, and you had something different in mind. So let's just proceed then, and perhaps next time, if there's new information, and that's what it learns me, please also give it to the Defence so that they can already raise the issue and say this is a different number of hours so you can inform the Chamber that this is a mistake. Let's ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. I asked these questions because I am looking at how to -- we lost one day last week due to the loss of voice of Mr. Harmon. I'm just wondering whether we could finish by not later than Friday, of course, which should be possible, even within the eight-hour schedule. But I would like to deal with some procedural issues as well, and therefore I had in mind if this six hours would be correct, then we might take tomorrow for the cross-examination, under the 60 per cent rule, which is not a strict rule but kind of a level of expectation by the Chamber, but I now understood that everything will take a bit more time. But if possible, the Chamber would very much like, since we will not be sitting for the next two weeks, to deal with the procedural issues by Friday, because otherwise we will have to come back on Monday where we are supposed not to sit, because, as I informed you, the Chamber agrees, under close monitoring, to start with the new schedule proposed, and it would be a pity if we would have to all come back on Monday to discuss this and a few more procedural issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't sound as if there's an enormous problem. If we assume the eight hours, I don't think Mr. Tieger's been suggesting he's likely to be more than the eight hours. I believe he feels reasonably comfortable about that, in which case we would begin cross-examination sometime in the middle of tomorrow. And Your Honour, at the moment, unless something unexpected turns up, and of course it often does, but unless something unexpected turns up, it looks as if we will manage to finish all these matters with some spare time for the other matters within this week. So perhaps I should just sit down now and let us do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So all the expectations are now again in the same direction, and I just take it for a typing error that I read six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, since it doesn't take any time while the witness is being fetched, can I just say, we don't quite understand what's happening if a schedule such as Your Honour has seems to reach Your Honour without falling into the hands of either Mr. Tieger, who is the person examining this witness, or us. Something's clearly going wrong in the administration somewhere. So I don't know. But clearly it's helpful both to Mr. Tieger and to me if we get these schedules updated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They stem from the Prosecution. And they're supposed to be given to the Defence and a copy to the Chamber, and the Defence could, if there's anything wrong with disclosure or translations, et cetera, they can at that very moment identify what they could expect to be used in court. And it's just something for proper preparation of the court hearings. But I do agree if the receiving part is the only one, that's the Chamber, who has knowledge of it, that's a bit odd. But I see the witness is waiting. Could we, Madam Usher, ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Okun. Good afternoon. Although I take it that it would even go without saying, it's my duty to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Ambassador Okun.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would like to begin today with something that you raised in your testimony yesterday. In response to a question about the number of Muslims who would live within territories held by the Bosnian Serbs, you referred to the removal of Muslims from the territory and the ethnic cleansing of Muslims by the Bosnian Serb forces. First, can I ask you about the sources of information that you and the Secretary Vance and the other negotiators had concerning the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from territories within Bosnia-Herzegovina by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first indication, and it was official and written, came from the plebiscite that the Bosnian Serb Assembly ordered in November 1991. This was a plebiscite of the Bosnian Serb people to decide whether to opt for remaining in a Bosnian Serb entity and also Yugoslavia. And one might have thought that there would just be a general plebiscite, you know, of the million and a quarter or so Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was not organised that way. It was organised opstina by opstina. And a very important, significant aspect was the decision written in the rules of the plebiscite that in any opstina where more than 50 per cent of the Serbs voted in favour of Republika Srpska, regardless of the size of the opstina, regardless of their percentage in the opstina, that opstina became part of the Republika Srpska. So for example, if you had an opstina that is arguendo, picture an opstina that has 10.000 voting population, 5.000 Bosnian Muslims, 3.000 Bosnian Serbs, 2.000 Bosnian Croats; 10.000. The 3.000 Bosnian Serbs vote out of 10.000. If 2.000 of them voted to remain in Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia, that opstina was automatically declared part of Republika Srpska, never mind that there are 7.000 others who don't want that. So that was the first indication, because what was to happen of those 7.000 people? They weren't just going to disappear by some magic trick. Then we had and noticed and saw the request for assistance, "assistance" from the JNA in December 1991 to "protect" the Bosnian Serb people in these places, in the plebiscitary areas, very similar to Croatia. The same game was being played. That was December 1991, and these were official documents. In January, Republika Srpska was proclaimed. January 9, as we all know. And in February, when the constitution of Republika Srpska was promulgated - this is February 1992 - it stated that the areas that were to comprise the territorial entity, the continuous territory, as was always emphasised to us by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and the others, that the areas would constitute all of these plebiscitary areas where regardless of the other numbers, a majority of Bosnian Serbs had voted to remain -- to join Yugoslavia, plus - and I believe I mentioned this yesterday - plus those areas where Serbs were in the minority because of the World War II genocide. So this was all written and known. And the question then arises, what was going to happen to the other people? What about the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, because in many of these opstinas, particularly along the Drina but others as well, the Bosnian Muslims in were the majority. Well, those so-called crisis committees played the same game as they did - a horrible game, I should say - as they did in Croatia. And this was physically known. Journalists saw it. When we travelled, infrequently I may say, but when we went to the areas, one could see the other populations being forcibly removed. So there was no secret about this. In fact, I believe the whole world knew this was happening, via television. I'm sorry to have to give you such a long answer, but I think it's important to know that this was already established by fiat and was not a spontaneous operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there organisations responsible for monitoring what was happening in those regions, and did you receive information from such organisations about what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first, we received quite detailed information from the EC Monitoring Mission, and then from the UNPROFOR troops as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the -- after the conflict erupted in -- with more intensity in April and May and June, did you receive information from such organisations as the ICRC, UNHCR, and others who had representatives in the region and were monitoring what was happening?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. By June, the camps were already being formed. Detention centres, large-scale detention centres, particularly in -- west of Banja Luka, around Prijedor; Trnopolje, a very, very big camp; the Omarska camp, which was much worse, a real concentration camp. These had already been formed, and there were thousands, thousands upon thousands of primarily Bosnian Muslims but also Bosnian Croats, civilians - civilians; men, women, and children - held in these centres. There then ensued quite a lengthy and painful discussion among the humanitarian agencies with the Bosnian Serb leadership about what to do with the people, because it was a terrible, moral dilemma. And it's in my diary notes; you'll see discussions with Madam Ogata, the head of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and with the senior officials of the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, because on the one hand they wanted to save these people, but on the other hand, removing them from the camps and taking them to Croatia, which was where most of them were going - they were not going back to their homes, they were being evacuated to Croatia - well, this was, as they said, collaborating in ethnic cleansing. And so that posed a very painful moral dilemma for the humanitarian organisations in the event they did take the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians under their wing into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, just to quickly identify one additional potential source, did you and Secretary Vance and the others involved in the negotiation also receive information from Tadeusz Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it confirmed what we had heard from others, yes, but he was also well aware and vitally concerned with Vance in his capacity as rapporteur on human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the information you were receiving from these various sources consistent?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was entirely consistent, I may say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you and Secretary Vance have occasions to let the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, know that you were aware of widespread ethnic cleansing or ongoing ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their response, Ambassador? Was there any meaningful attempt to deny that cleansing had taken place or was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't deny it. The typical, indeed, the almost invariable response was to point out the genocide that had been practiced against the Serbs in World War II and earlier periods, or to point to crimes that were allegedly being committed in -- at the present time, 1992 and 1993, 1991, whatever, mostly in 1992 and 1993, that were crimes against them. For example, if we would raise the question of the shelling of Sarajevo, the Bosnian Serb leadership would normally reply, "Oh, but we're only doing that to protect our own people. Sarajevo is the biggest concentration camp in Bosnia-Herzegovina. 60.000 Serbs are being held hostage by the Muslims." There was no evidence for that, but that was the standard Bosnian Serb response. It was very much tu quoque; you're another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, just to clarify the written record, you indicated that the almost invariable response was to either point to genocide or World War II, or to point crimes that were allegedly being committed at the present time, and that thought was not completed. Did that mean crimes that were being committed at the present time against Serbs by the Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand that response to be, in effect, an acknowledgment that the Bosnian Serbs, too, were committing crimes, but to point the negotiators to the fact that others were doing the same?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb leadership, during the course of your negotiations, take negotiating positions that depended upon the change in demographic conditions that had been produced by the ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly. Their whole claim, for example, for the Drina River valley, that is to say for the left bank of the Drina, was based on ethnic cleansing. I mean, they knew it; we knew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, indicate to you and Secretary Vance and the other negotiators that the use of force would cease as soon as the Bosnian Serbs got what they wanted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they thereby indicating to you and to Secretary Vance and the others that they were in control of the forces that were engaged in the cleansings, running the camps, and so on?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, Dr. Karadzic said explicitly, and I've quoted him actually somewhere in the diary, that he controlled - we -- I and the Bosnian Serb civilian leadership - we control General Mladic, we control the military. And he went on to say "You know how the soldiers are. They don't like to be controlled by civilians, but we control them." He was quite explicit on that point. And also, we saw it in other cases. Just to give one example: When the issue arose of creating a no-fly zone over Bosnia similar to the no-fly zones over Iraq - this was 1992 - at one meeting between Dr. Karadzic, Lord Owen, and myself, just the three of us in the room, we again were insisting on the Bosnian Serbs stopping this practice, and Dr. Karadzic offered to fly the planes, the war planes of the VRS, which were based at Banja Luka airport, he offered to fly them to Belgrade. And so we said that might be acceptable. And in our presence, he took out his cell phone and called the commander, the military commander, of the Banja Luka airfield and told him to remove the planes -- well, I shouldn't say he told him to remove; they discussed the possibility of the planes being removed, which showed - and this was in the evening, by the way - this showed that the ease of communication, the rapidity of communication, the fact that the communication was open between the Bosnian Serb leadership and some nameless air force colonel of the VRS at the Banja Luka airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Yesterday, you made reference to the Cutileiro plan which was ongoing from at least February 1992. And I believe you also referred to the 12 May 1992 statement of strategic objectives. I'd like to quickly show you those documents, and then I have a question for you in connection with those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if the ambassador could be shown both the proposed Cutileiro plan with the attached map, and then the strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I know by now that if we're talking about the Cutileiro plan, we have to carefully look at whether we have the Lisbon version or the - what was the other one? - Sarajevo version. Which one is on the table at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Lisbon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lisbon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, before I proceed with the specific question, let me ask you a quick question about the 12 May 1992 document, the strategic objectives. Although the numbers are the same, is it correct that that document is not to be confused with the six political goals or war aims that you described yesterday; that, while related, they are different?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They are not meant to be nor are they identical. The six principles of May 12, the strategic objectives, concern almost exclusively territory. They were about land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, forgive me for this clarification, for amending my supposed clarification, but before anyone else notices, I see that the Cutileiro plan before the witness and before the Court is dated 18 March, 1992, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that. And the other thing we have to do is to check whether the map attached to it is the Sarajevo map or the Lisbon map. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, there has been a suggestion in this case that there's a close correlation between the Cutileiro plan and the strategic objectives. And I would like to know from you whether you share that assessment or whether you see significant distinctions between the two.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's not a close relationship. There is a relationship insofar as it discusses the three constituent peoples and would give each of the three peoples, the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs, would give them a juridical identity. But you can see from the map that we are looking at that it does not grant territorial continuity to Republika Srpska. The areas that are on this map that are entirely white are the Serb areas, and they are disconnected. For example, in along the Posavina. Also, one sees from the map that most of the Drina is given on the correct, that's to say the census, basis of the ethnicities. And all the striped areas are Muslim opstinas, from Bijeljina down almost to Nevesinje, which conforms to the ethnic reality. That's the population of Bosnia in 1991. So that definitely does not conform with the strategic objectives. And there are other points as well. The Bosnian Serb border is not pushed as far as the Neretva. So there are some conformities, but by and large, the Henry Darwin map, the map for Cutileiro plan which was drawn up by Mr. Darwin, did not carry out these objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Cutileiro plan call for the establishment of a corridor linking Serbia to the Krajina, as the strategic objectives do?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge. One has to bear in mind that the Cutileiro plan died aborning. It never was completed. This map, for example, that we're looking at was discussed quite heavily but remained a draft proposal unless it was definitively rejected. And the plan was always a work in progress. Indeed, if you look at the last page over the date Sarajevo, 18 March, the last sentence reads, and I quote from the Cutileiro plan paper: "This paper is the basis of further negotiations." So it was clear that this was a discussion paper. It was not a complete and formal plan. It was serious, of course. But one cannot really give it the same status as a formal plan proposed to the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Cutileiro plan call for the physical division of Sarajevo into Muslim and Serb parts, separate parts with people segregated?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Ambassador, was the Cutileiro plan intended as a proposed that would be implemented by agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there was no question of that. In fact, the three parties did agree to this tentative document in March of 1992, and then the Bosnian government withdraw its signature at the very end of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that also represent a significant difference between the strategic objectives and the Cutileiro plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the fact that the Cutileiro plan anticipated implementation by agreement also reflect the significant distinction between it and the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes, because given the extreme nature of the demands in the strategic objectives of May 12, given the fact that they were claiming territory in some cases that was overwhelmingly non-Serb - along the Drina, for example - that it was based on a unilateral assertion of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, could we now turn back to some of the specific entries in your diary. And I'd like to turn your attention first to a diary entry of September 10th.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what year, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. It just may be worth mentioning, I think we're right that the page from the Official Gazette, this is a previous exhibit, of course, is P47. If that's right, if that's agreed to be the number, I think it's probably helpful to put that on the transcript so that subsequently when anybody is looking at the transcript they know what it is we're talking about. And the other document I'm afraid we don't remember immediately the number, but the other document is part of a Defence exhibit. We think it's 5 or 6. It seems it may be 5. We've understood Ms. Philpott to be saying it is 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map has a separate number. The map is D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 7, thank you, Your Honours. It's just helpful for the future for all of us, I think, to have it there in the transcript in the same passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to make it clear, Mr. Stewart, D5 is the statement of principles, and we have another statement of principles under D6. And the map, I think we switched from a more general map which was first introduced, not as detailed as this one, and then -- at least the detailed one is admitted under D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's all as we understand it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears that we're having some difficulties with the Sanction system, so I think we're going to have to place this diary entry on the ELMO, the physical copy. If we could have the first page of that entry placed on the ELMO, that would be R0163902.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, as indicated by your entry, this is a meeting with Dr. Karadzic and Colonel Zarkovic, and the note taker. And we see on that first page a map depicted. Can you explain to us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean page that ends in 902 from my diary journal, that map? Yes. Dr. Karadzic -- I will read what I wrote: Pulls out Darwin's detailed map. And that would be the map that we just discussed, the Cutileiro map of March. Pulls out Darwin's detailed map, and then he had an overlay showing the Serb-controlled areas. And I drew by hand, and I apologise, I'm not a cartographer, I draw by hand his overlay which showed the Serb-controlled areas. And basically, it's the Drina up to Semberija and Bijeljina, and then the Posavina corridor, and then the -- and Western Bosnia, which was Bosnian controlled, and the white area was that held by the Muslims and the Croats. And basically, that's the Cazinska Krajina, what came to be called during the conflict, the Bihac pocket, and Central Bosnia. So this was his overlay, and he was telling us "We already control this area." It was a straightforward presentation of what the Bosnian Serb forces, the VRS and the irregulars, held at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can ask you then to turn to the two pages that are contained on the ERN marked page R0163904, continuation of the notes from that meeting, and the entry at the top left of that page is "CRV - about camps."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Secretary Vance was going to ask him about the detention centres, the concentration camps particularly in the western part of Bosnia. And Dr. Karadzic replied, as he usually did, Sarajevo is the biggest camp of all. 60.000 Serbs are held prison there, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. I mean, this was a standard response, which is why after 60.000 I just wrote -- you see the three dots, meaning we've heard this before and there's no need to repeat this argument. It was the standard argument. Then he -- Secretary Vance mentioned that we've spoken to the ICRC, and Dr. Karadzic says that Trnopolje, which was one of the very large and quite infamous camps, is an open camp, by which he meant that people are free to enter it and leave it. That is, the displaced Bosnian Muslims and Croats were free, he was saying, to enter the camp or to leave the camp. In fact, that was not true. Then Lord Owen says, we need to phase this out. This camp has to be ended, this situation must end. And Karadzic again goes back to helping the Serbs detained in camps by others. And that was true. There were Bosnian Serbs being held by the others. There was no doubt of that. They were held in much, much smaller number, but they were also being held. So as a matter of fact, that existed, but the quantity was overwhelmingly different. I mean, there was just no question about the quantity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the following page of your diary, but the same ERN page reference, you tell Dr. Karadzic, "You shelled Sarajevo first." What prompted that remark by you, and what was Dr. Karadzic's response?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, as you see by the previous statement, the one beginning "Why are sanctions tightened" he was appealing for our sympathy. He did that fairly often. He would play the role of the innocent party, the injured party, when we knew and he knew, and he knew that we knew, he was not the innocent party. His people started this whole thing. So he's complaining here. He's lamenting the fact. And he points out that the Croatians, both in the Krajina and in Bosnia, are getting weapons in spite of the arms embargo that had been passed by the Security Council already in September 1991. And being a little tired of hearing this litany, because it wasted our time, among other things, I basically was saying to him, look, you know, stop this kind of talk. We all know the facts of the situation. You're talking about the Croats getting arms. You're shelling Sarajevo mercilessly, thousands of shells a day were falling on Sarajevo. And this meeting was taking place in Sarajevo. You notice along the side I write "constant firing" with arrows. You see that on the page. I wrote fire. We could hear the shells falling as we were conducting this meeting in Sarajevo. And here is Dr. Karadzic bemoaning the fact that, you know, that other people are getting weapons. I mean, this was really quite an anomalous picture. We are sitting in Sarajevo, the Bosnian Serbs are shelling the city, we are being shelled. We're sitting with flak jackets on, helmets, and Dr. Karadzic is complaining. So I said, come on, Dr. Karadzic, we all know who shelled Sarajevo first. And then his answer to that was, "They started the war" - "they" being the Bosnian Muslims - "by expelling me from my apartment in Sarajevo." "They started the war by expelling me from my apartment in Sarajevo." Thousands of people have been by this time killed, hundreds of thousands displaced from their homes, and Dr. Karadzic thinks it is a convincing argument to tell the negotiators that the Muslims started the war by expelling him from his apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and the rest of the negotiating team obtain estimates of the number of shells that were being fired into Sarajevo by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Once the UN observers were there in decent number, which was the summer of 1992, they kept a shell count throughout the entire period. And I had actually in my office in Geneva, at the conference, I had a graph on the wall that listed chronologically, day by day, the shell count from the Bosnian Serb side and the return fire from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to recall those numbers, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Serb shell count averaged three to five thousand per day. The number of shells landing in Sarajevo area was between -- normally between three and five thousand per day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me ask you to turn next to a diary entry of September 17th. It is found at ERN number R0163950.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what date is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. September 17th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What page? Could you give me the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you can turn first to the page which is the second page of your diary entry and is located at the ERN range R0163951.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of the page, at the left, there's an entry which indicates that CRV, Secretary Vance, indicated that all must have right of return, cannot support ethnic cleansing. Can you tell us about that exchange and what Dr. Karadzic explained in response.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what Secretary Vance was saying, was acknowledging the fact, as I mentioned a few moments ago, that the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats who had been forcibly expelled from their homes, that he was saying that these people should be allowed to return to their homes. And he says we cannot support ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Dr. Karadzic's response indicated below?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic typically does not deny the ethnic cleansing, but responds "Nor should you support the taking of ethnic hostages." What I wrote was "nor ethnic hostages." People are being held in certain areas against their will. He meant Serb people. Sarajevo, Zenica, Tuzla. So his response was not to deny the ethnic cleansing, not to even discuss the question of allowing the forcibly expelled Muslims and Croat population to return, but rather to say that the Bosnian Serbs should be allowed to leave the -- certain areas presumably so they could go to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the diary entry indicates that DLO, or Lord Owen, I take it, entered the room, and according to the entry, observes that Dr. Karadzic must realise that the siege of Sarajevo does you - that is the Bosnian Serbs - immense harm, to which Dr. Karadzic responded, "Not a siege, protecting our suburbs." Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There it is. That's what he said. He denied that it was a siege. It obviously was a siege. Serb forces surrounded the city. The only way in or out of Sarajevo at this period was through Serb lines and with Serb permission. Now, the Muslims did, in fact, build a tunnel near the airport, so people sneaked in and out through this tunnel, but the city was, in fact, besieged. It was surrounded on all sides by Bosnian Serb forces who controlled ingress and egress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to a couple of additional entries, Ambassador. On the next page of your diary, although it's located at the same ERN page, toward the bottom of that page, there's a comment by Dr. Karadzic concerning the percentage of Serbs in Sarajevo, and then he indicates, "I could persuade Serbs to remain if we had two entities in Sarajevo. Will take time, antagonism too great."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the standard refrain of the Bosnian leadership; to divide Sarajevo into two separate cities, you know, like East Berlin and West Berlin, or Nicosia. To divide it into a Bosnian Serb section and a Bosnian Muslim section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And consistent with that, if I could ask you to turn to the next page, which is R0163952, at the diary entry on the right side of the page, in the middle of that page, there's another reference to a comment by Dr. Karadzic: "The communities cannot live together at present. Too much hate."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the position of the Bosnian Serbs throughout the whole period. That the communities, the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be separated, that they could not live together. Now, again, it has to be borne in mind that very large sections, most of Bosnia, was thoroughly intermixed. This was not a physical area which, while it had 44 per cent Muslim population, 31 per cent Serb, 19, 20 Croat, et cetera, that the people already were living apart. They were thoroughly intermixed and -- but the burden of that remark, which was consistent with the Bosnian Serb leadership, was that they had to be taken apart; and that, of course, is what ethnic cleansing was designed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership not only with respect to Sarajevo, but with respect to the territories within Bosnia that they claimed as Serbian land?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. I go back to the point you made earlier when Dr. Karadzic put the overlay on Henry Darwin's map for Cutileiro. We just discussed a few moments ago. He showed the entire Drina, the entire Drina and as far west as the Neretva River, as Serb, whereas on the ethnic map, most of that area, probably half of it anyway, were majority Muslim opstinas. Well, how did that happen? I mean, how did they go from being Muslim opstinas to Serb opstinas? We know how that happened: The Muslim population was forced out. Or worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you've referred to the ethnic composition or the demographic composition of the area in the Drina. I'd like to have this map marked as Prosecution's exhibit next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P211.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, first let me ask you if you're familiar with this map.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It's an ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would say based on the 1991 census. Yes, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that map assist in describing the demographic composition of the Drina area and other parts of Bosnia that you were referring to during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. You can -- the green is Muslim. The red and pink is ethnic Serb. The blue is Croat. And you see all the green. These are majority Muslim opstinas: Foca, Gorazde, Rogatica, Visegrad, et cetera. Srebrenica. Some names are quite well known. And these were Muslim majority provinces, based on the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one thing. Mr. Krajisnik, I can imagine that the line of sight is a bit disturbed. It's also shown on your screen if you choose the "video monitor." Then you see exactly what the witness is pointing at. Not at this very moment, but as soon as he restarts, because you might have seen yourself at that very moment. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move away from the map in my next question. So if it's helpful to refocus on the map for a moment, we can ask the technician to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will do so. Mr. Krajisnik, were you able to sufficiently follow the...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am able to follow, although this is the wrong map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's the map that is presented to the witness by the Prosecution, Mr. Krajisnik. So whether right or wrong is a different matter, but we'll hear from Defence counsel if there's anything wrong with the map. So there's no need to repeat the pointing done by the witness. Yes. I take it that your hand sign is to be understood that you do not like the witness to repeat the pointing at the map. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you indicated that you were familiar with that map. Was that a map that you had available to you during the course of your efforts, negotiating efforts?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of them. We had many. There are others that show the same figures in different ways. The Bosnian Serb leadership preferred another map which purported to show their control, as they called it, their control of 65 per cent of the land. This was based on the contention, which was not always incorrect, that the Bosnian Serb population of Bosnia and Herzegovina tended to be more rural than urban. And the Muslim and Croat was somewhat more urban. Therefore, they had more farmers, and the farmers had certain land. They also claimed as part of that 65 per cent control all of the national parks and all of the federal Yugoslav installations for themselves. That is to say, if there was a national park somewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they would say, well, you see, that makes it Yugoslavia, and therefore it's Serb territory. And they had maps that showed that, you see. But they were all based on the same statistics, which were not in doubt. It's the census of 1981, which was the last complete census, and the census of 1991 - the decennial censuses in Yugoslavia were taken in 1981 and 1991 - the 1991 census did not differ in any material way from the 1981 census. The only point was that since the fighting began very shortly thereafter, the 1991 census was never officialised. So if one wants to be very technical and speak of the last official census, one takes the 1981 figures. But as I say, the 1991 figures were almost identical to the 1981 figures. But this was a standard map, and there are other standard maps. But some do emphasise different factors. I mean, if you have a map, for example, physical map, you see much more of the geography. We had economic maps. Where were the dams located? Where were the mines, that sort of thing. Where was the electrical grid? So we had lots of maps, and this is an accurate ethnic map of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me turn for a moment to the objective of the Bosnian Serb leaders to see that Sarajevo was physically divided into a Serbian part and a Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I just wonder, if we're leaving the map, there are two things: First of all, I think Madam Usher probably doesn't have to stand there like a Christmas tree indefinitely and could be relieved of standing there with the map, which then ties in with the next suggestion: I wonder perhaps if the map could then be handed to Mr. Krajisnik so that he can have an opportunity of looking at it a bit more closely. Kill two birds with one stone, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you still need the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it temporarily be given to Mr. Krajisnik to further inspect it. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was also, just on a purely practical level as far as the maps are concerned, we have been supplied with -- as I understand, we have been supplied with this map and a number of other maps in electronic form, which are coloured, and we can certainly print them off in colour, and obviously we can't print them in that handy slip-in-your-pocket size that we see behind us for the exhibit. But I don't know, if the Prosecution do have a colour version of that and if they do have access to a colour photocopier, it would seem that in relation to this sort of exhibit that a simple batch of colour copies for the Bench and for the Defence team and everybody else would be a reasonable and practical request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's a suggestion. I take it that you'll reflect on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not expect you to immediately produce now the small photocopies, but it's a suggestion which makes quite some sense. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I indicated that I wanted to return to your testimony about the objective of the Bosnian Serb leaders to physically divide Sarajevo into Serbian parts, a Serbian part and a Muslim part where Serbs would live and Muslims would live separately. Did you become aware of efforts by Bosnian Serb forces to forcibly achieve this objective during this rough time period, in the summer and fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the shelling was all about. The shelling was designed to create a -- you know, a wall of fire, if you will. I don't want to be melodramatic, but the shelling in effect provided a wall of fire between the communities. That's what it was designed to do. The shelling was directed. This was not erratic, unaimed fire. Dr. Karadzic would point that out to us. He would say, for example, after we divide the city, you know, it will be all right for the Muslims to live in, and then he would list two or three areas. So the shelling was part and parcel of the effort to divide the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And more specifically, did you receive information during the summer and fall of 1992 that efforts to forcibly remove, or efforts to expel Muslims from portions of Sarajevo had been successful?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intermittently, but not very much. That was not a major factor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the extent that such information was received and you were aware of some successful efforts to achieve the physical separation of Sarajevo, was it your understanding from your discussions with the Bosnian Serb leaders and from the other information you received that the shelling was also a way of ensuring the preservation of that change in the demographics, of ensuring that the ethnic cleansing was preserved?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point, yes. The shelling had several objectives. Why does one shell a capital city? I mean, let us start with ABCs. Of course, it's not only an act of war, but shelling any civilian area and doing it month after month after month is very serious business, forbidden by the laws of war, in fact. International humanitarian law is quite clear on that. So what was the purpose? Well, this was the seat of the Bosnian Muslim government, so the first goal was to frighten them, to terrorise them, to make them know they were surrounded; in other words, to induce a feeling of hopelessness in the Bosnian Muslim government leadership. The next goal, as I mentioned, was to utilise the shelling physically to divide the city the way they wished it to be divided. And finally, I would think that the goal was to animate the Bosnian Serb population, to show them that their army was powerful, that they could do what they want, even to Sarajevo. Now, I can't prove that last point because they didn't say that. But it's hard to imagine actually why the shelling continued throughout this whole war. As Lord Owen pointed out, you, Mr. Counsel, pointed it out just a moment ago, as Lord Owen said to Karadzic, this shelling does you no good. It's the single thing that brings obloquy, that brings disgrace, he would say, on your cause. Surely you must know that. That did not matter to Bosnian Serb leadership. So they clearly must have had some reason for doing it, and I've just mentioned three possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to turn next to your diary entries of September 18th, the following day. That entry is contained at ERN number Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. R0163960 and the subsequent pages. Just a handful of entries I would like to draw your attention to, Ambassador. The first one is found at the bottom of the first diary page and reflects comments by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Insofar as I can, if I'm reading it correctly, it says: "Recognition led to war. Will also happen in Macedonia if it is recognised." Can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what he was saying is that the recognition of Bosnia as a sovereign, independent country by the European Community and by the United States, and then its subsequent admission to the United Nations, all of which happened in the spring of 1992, that this act led to war. Now, Macedonia was not recognised because of -- by the EC or the US because of the problem that Greece had with the name. It was later resolved. But he then goes on to say, "This will also happen in Macedonia if it's recognised." War would result also in Macedonia if it were recognised, because Macedonia was a very sensitive area to the Serbs. In fact, it had been part of Serbia until 1946 when Tito removed Macedonia and created the Republic of Macedonia. It was always, until then, called Southern Serbia. So the Serbs had a great deal of interest in Macedonia and many attachments to it. For example, the Serbian Orthodox church never recognise the creation of the Macedonian Orthodox church. Just a point, even though it's the same religion. And here we have Dr. Karadzic saying that because Macedonia is so sensitive, if it's recognised, war will result. Well, the fact of the matter is that some time later, not much time later, Macedonia was recognised, and no war resulted whatsoever. There was no war between Serbia and Macedonians or between the Serbs in Macedonia or the JNA or anything else. It was entirely peaceful. And I think one can, without exaggeration, draw the conclusion from this that the war in Bosnia was not inevitable. Here is Dr. Karadzic telling us that war is inevitable in Macedonia, as it turned out to be in Bosnia, and that was not the case at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina was something that Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders had indicated previously was a factor they could not and would not accept?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They would not accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the next page of your diary contained on the same ERN page, Dr. Karadzic makes the comment, "The Muslim side will soon be dominant with more than 50 per cent." Then there's a subsequent comment by Dr. Koljevic: "Serbs need territorial and functional autonomy." You then note that Secretary Vance asks about territorial versus political autonomy. And Drs. Karadzic and Koljevic indicate that that's in the context of handing back some land to Muslims. Can you explain that exchange to us, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That entire exchange is about the question of what kind of governance would there be in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this was a recurring theme. And they say again, as they say repeatedly, that neither the Serbs nor the Bosnian Croats would accept a unitary Bosnian state, that is to say a one man, one vote state. They will not accept a state based on one man, one vote. That's why they're worried that the Muslims would soon, for demographic reasons, be more than 50 per cent. So they say again here, we need our own state with our own territory, with our own people, and our own laws. That's what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, before I turn to the entries I wanted to draw your attention to on the following page, I also wanted to confirm the attendance at that meeting. Is it correct that that meeting was attended by Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Buha, and Mr. Misa Milosevic for the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; Karadzic, Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, Aleksa Buha, and Misa Milosevic. That's Misa, not to be confused with Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the conversation or discussion continued, and we see it reflected on the following page at R0163961, Dr. Koljevic says that they need to put all the cards on the table, not get lost in mazes, nuances, and subtleties. And then he goes on to describe what is acceptable or unacceptable to the Bosnian Serbs. Can you explain that exchange to us, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he -- after showing off his excellent English with "mazes, nuances, and subtleties," he says, "Serbs will not accept the internal borders" - meaning the internal borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina - "without some form of cantonisation." That is to say, without a Serb-governed area, not something subject to Muslims. But the Serbs are prepared to accept and prefer agreed change in the internal borders to accommodate ethnic realities. Well, the phrase "to accommodate ethnic realities" is a very clear, not-so-subtle reference to the ethnic cleansing, because this conversation was held in September 1992 and by September of 1992, already hundreds of thousands of Bosnian Muslims had been forcibly displaced from their homes to -- in order to make Republika Srpska pure, or as pure as the Serb Army could make it. And so he says, fine, sure, we'll accept changes in internal borders provided they accommodate the ethnic realities. What he's doing there is stating in words what Dr. Karadzic did when he put the overlay on the ethnic map of Bosnia, the one I drew by hand. He's saying, "This is the area controlled now by the VRS." You know, there are very few other ethnicities in this area. That's the accommodation of ethnic realities. So that's what he said. Fine, if you want to make this kind of -- we'll accept that. We will certainly accept that, a map drawn on the situation that exists now, post ethnic cleansing. And then he goes on to say, and this was another standard Bosnian Serb refrain: "We are not prepared to accept Tito's borders. Bosnia-Herzegovina `is a pure Bolshevik creation'." And that's really almost ludicrously amusing to make that statement, because in fact, the borders of Bosnia are among the oldest not just in south-western Europe but in all of Europe. If you look, for example, at a Habsburg map of 1878, the map that was used at the Congress of Berlin when Austria-Hungary was given co-sovereignty with the Ottoman empire over Bosnia-Herzegovina. Until 1878, it was Turkish, but in 1878, following the Turkish defeat in the Bulgarian war and the Treaty at San Stefano, Bismarck divided that part of the empire between the Austrians and the Turks. If you look at the map that was used, the borders haven't changed hardly at all. It's a very old, established border, the ones of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were not Tito's borders. So, you know, this is the kind of debating point that we heard quite a lot, I must say, from the Bosnian Serb leadership. They may have believed it, for all I know, but it had no validity and it bore no relationship to reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I note the time, and I think it's an appropriate moment for our recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just going to invite you to find a suitable moment. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I do understand that the excerpts you've provided from the diaries are from a different bundle as presented yesterday, that is, it is a new set, two binders which have not yet received a number, I think, and which at least the Judges have not received. We're not inviting you to immediately hand them over, but just for purposes of the record. Madam Registrar, the two new binders would have number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are we using them later on, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the binders that have just been marked P212 in fact contain the diary entries we're referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just to clarify, if I may, the first binder contained diary entries reflecting meetings related to the Conference on Yugoslavia, which lasted roughly until August of 1992, although the diary entries don't go that long. These two binders that have now been marked as P212 reflect entries related to the International Conference on Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the index, we see that they contain the diaries numbers from 1 until 9, diaries described as Diary of ICFY. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can I ask you to turn next to your diary entries of September 19th, 1992. That is reflected at page bearing ERN number R0163971 and the following page.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, it appears that the Sanction programme is, at least for now, working again and should obviate the need for the ELMO at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, this is a meeting in Geneva attended by, according to the heading at the top, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, and Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Misa Milosevic. And I'd like to direct your attention to a few entries. First, at the bottom of the first page, there are comments by Dr. Karadzic: "We do not need war. We should stop and stay where they and we are." Any comment on that, Ambassador? Anything that you need to add that you haven't already explained about the nature of the negotiations and the information --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. What Dr. Karadzic was saying here reflected the fact that by September of 1992, the VRS, the Bosnian Serb Army, the Bosnian irregulars, had conquered and controlled about 70 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So he was saying we should stop now. Obviously, it was to their advantage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next page, the second entry indicates Dr. Koljevic saying, "You need to put pressure on the Muslims if you want to stop the fighting. But international community has not done this." What was the pressure aimed at getting the Muslims to do? What did Dr. Koljevic ask you as representatives of the international community to get the Muslims to do in order to stop the fighting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what he would have wished was that we, as negotiators, convince the Muslims to sign a peace based on the current territorial holdings, the current situation, which it goes without saying they would not do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two more entries I'd like to bring your attention to: The first appears immediately below the remarks to which you just referred. It's Dr. Karadzic saying, or as reflected in your entry, "continuous emphasis on ethnically based territorial units."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my gloss of what he was saying. I mean, he's not saying that. He goes on and on. This is a meeting that lasted almost two hours, and you notice that I've covered one hour and 25 minutes in two pages. Now, if you had a transcript of that, it would probably run, I suppose, 20 or 30 pages. But I didn't have to write everything down because Dr. Karadzic is saying what Dr. Karadzic always says, so I write "continuous emphasis on ethnically based territorial units." He may have spoken for 5 or 10 minutes on that subject; that is to say, we have to have, you know, ethnically pure, we can't live together, they hate us, we hate -- you know, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. This was the same old story. So I just note that "continued emphasis on ethnically based territorial units." But it's important to note that there is no deviation in the Bosnian Serb position. Indeed, there was no deviation throughout the months and months of negotiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just below that entry, it appears that Dr. Koljevic is underscoring the need for physical separation and the inability, in his view, of the Serbs and Muslims to live together, where he says, "War has shattered trust. Communities cannot live together any more. To deny that is fantasy."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was part of the standard line. No trust. Hatred between the communities. And then again, I notice in parenthesis at the bottom, a lengthy expatiation on those points, again, by Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic. The elaborations went on at great length.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any deviation from this position by any of the Bosnian Serb leaders present?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. They were all consistent on that, and they all said the same thing. Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic, Buha, Lukic. Buha and Lukic were somewhat cruder in their presentations. That just reflects their personalities. But the top leaders, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic, were very consistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can we turn next to the diary entry of September 24th, 1992, found at ERN R0163985. This appears to be a morning meeting with Dr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to assist the Court in understanding the diary entries, below the entry noting Dr. Koljevic's presence, there's some initials of others also present. Can you just identify who those people are because their initials appear repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: CRV is Cyrus Vance. DLO is Lord Owen. HSO is me. PH is Peter Hall, Ambassador Hall, Owen's deputy. MA is Martti Ahtissari, who was the chairman of one of our working groups on Bosnia. And FE is Fred Eckhardt, who was the spokesman for the conference. He is now the spokesman for the Secretary-General of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this meeting, we see the first entry by -- remarks by Secretary Vance about BL. Can you explain what was the subject of that meeting and what discussion ensued.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the previous page, you'll see I wrote and underlined "Problem, Banja Luka ethnic cleansing." We had received confirmed reports of serious ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka. Now, as we all know, Banja Luka's a major city. It's the second-largest city in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not that that is alone the issue, but still if it's major and a major city, there's a lot of ethnic cleansing going on. So the day began at 10.30 when we met with the Yugoslav Ambassador, Pavicevic, who admitted, acknowledged that it was going on. You see Ambassador P, "It must be stopped," meaning we must stop the Bosnian Serb's ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka. This is the Yugoslav Ambassador talking. "I will call Belgrade. I will speak to Cosic and Milosevic. I will do everything I can." So after we met with him briefly, we met with Koljevic for almost an hour. And again, the principal subject was how to stop the Bosnian Serb ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka. What to do about this situation? And again, Koljevic does not deny it. When Vance says to him, what do you hear about this? He says: "Banja Luka's under control. The problem is Prijedor." Okay, so he's telling us that their ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka is not so bad, it's bad in Prijedor, et cetera. And Koljevic volunteers to call Karadzic, and the meeting proceeds from there. As it turned out, Dr. Karadzic wished to have Secretary Vance join him in Banja Luka, and Vance and Owen did go to Banja Luka. I did not go with them. I had to look after the conference. Vance and Owen did go to Banja Luka and were able to confirm the ethnic cleansing, but at the same time, by their presence, they did succeed in temporarily slowing the ethnic cleansing. They did not stop it, but their personal presence there ameliorated for a bit the condition of the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, who were being forcibly expelled from Banja Luka. Mosques were being blown up. The Catholic churches were being destroyed. It was a very serious situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the diary indicates that Dr. Koljevic indicated that he or someone else would contact the chief of police in the area, and later on on the same page the diary entry indicates Dr. Koljevic spoke to the regional chief of police. During discussions with the Bosnian Serb leaders about activities in the municipalities, did they indicate that with respect to areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina over which they claimed control, that they had subordinate political and police officials there who were in charge of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, certainly yes. This is an indication. Koljevic goes out of the room, comes back and says, "I've spoken to the regional chief of police." That was -- there's no question of that. Just as I mentioned earlier, Karadzic, in my presence, called up the colonel in charge of the Yugoslav air force -- actually, at that point, I suppose the VRS air force, but these were Yugoslav planes, in Banja Luka in my presence. So there was no question that they had direct control of these people. That was self-evident. I mean, they did have the control, and they showed it frequently. And this was one case in point. He leaves the room, makes a telephone call, and comes back and tells us that I - Nikola Koljevic - have just spoken to the regional chief of police, and then goes on to tell us another fairy tale, if you see the rest of the diary entry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that in a moment. But one question more, and that is, did the Bosnian Serb leaders appear to have any more difficulty communicating with their municipal subordinates and police subordinates than with the military officials in the manner you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I never saw any indication of that. They all carried cell phones. They never said ever "We've tried to reach Dusan and we couldn't find -- we couldn't speak with him." Any time they said they needed to talk to somebody, they talked to that person. I mean, one sees that in the diaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that Dr. Koljevic returned to the meeting and went on to tell you and the others another fairy tale. Can you tell us what that was, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phrase masquerading. One of the standard ripostes of the Bosnian Serb leadership when we would tax them with the abuses and rapes and expulsions being carried out by the Bosnian Serbs, they would frequently say, no, the Muslims have stolen our uniforms and are masquerading as Serbs in VRS uniforms. So they -- it is Muslims dressed in Serb uniforms who are raping Muslim women, that sort of something. So we would hear that frequently, so I write "masquerading, massacring Serbs, training camps," that sort of thing. This was the standard response, always to blame the other side. Bear in mind, the subject was ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka. And Koljevic doesn't -- never says "it's not happening. We're not doing it. The press is lying. We are hearing distorted information." He never says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can I next ask you to turn to a diary entry of September 30th, 1992. That's found at ERN R0164015. Now, Ambassador, let me direct your attention to a few entries during that meeting. First, the -- your notes indicate it's a meeting with Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic, and then you indicate the initials of the negotiators also present. At the early phase of the meeting, Lord Owen indicates that there is outrage in respect of a story in the New York Times on Brcko killings early in May and June, and he indicates, "Let's get on with solving this," followed by a response by Dr. Karadzic, "We're not besieging Sarajevo," and I should mention there's reference to Sarajevo earlier in Lord Owen's comments. On the following page, at ERN R0164016, Dr. Karadzic continues about Sarajevo, "We have not conquered Sarajevo, could have, et cetera." Then according to your notes, Lord Owen, and it says "shuts Kara up." Dr. Karadzic responds: "We're the underdog. Cannot allow humanitarian aid to hurt us militarily." And then you explain something about Morillon's plan, UNPROFOR headquarters at Ilidza, et cetera, and Dr. Karadzic says, "We cannot give up Ilidza, et cetera, our wounded have died. Et cetera." Ambassador Okun, any comments that might be of assistance to the Court in appreciating the significance of those exchanges.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. The discussion here referred basically to the negotiators trying to accommodate Karadzic's repeated requests that Bosnian Serbs who wished to leave Sarajevo be allowed to do so. You'll recall he makes quite a lot of the fact that they are being held hostage, constantly claiming 60.000, 70.000 Bosnian Serbs are being held hostage in Sarajevo; it's the biggest concentration camp in Bosnia, et cetera, et cetera. That's his common line. We've seen plenty of that. So the negotiators took him up on that, and General Morillon had a plan to get them out if they wanted to leave. As it happened, nothing ever came of it because all of Karadzic's talk about the Bosnian Serbs' desire to flee Sarajevo was just talk, and when the negotiators and the UNPROFOR people on the ground offered to take them out, they never did; that is to say, the Bosnian Serbs did not take up the offer en masse. So this was a fruitless discussion. But it indicated once more that the position taken by Karadzic and the entire Bosnian Serb leadership was not, to put it charitably, was not based on a fair appreciation of how to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can we next turn to your diary entry of October 11th, 1992, found at ERN R0164042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we in one way or another expedite the distribution of documents because we start walking when you are about to ask questions, and then it takes us one minute or one minute and a half to get everyone a copy. Could we either -- well, I leave it to your imagination how to expedite the matter. Whatever is left over at the end of the day will be returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see I'm now provided with a translation in B/C/S of the last distributed entry, but the previous one was not -- there was no translation. May I take it that Mr. Karadzic got one or -- pardon me, Mr. Karadzic. I've heard so much about him. Mr. Krajisnik, did you receive a translation of the previous entry, that's the entry of September 30th? The last one distributed was the October 10th, at least.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was following in English, so I hadn't checked that out. But it doesn't matter. It needn't be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed then, Mr. Tieger. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, there are just a couple of references I wanted to ask you about in connection with the October 11th meeting with Dr. Karadzic. There's an asterisk on the first page next to the entry "Talks with Croats progressing. If so --" and "Muslims cannot fight without Croats," and then if you could read for us the two words in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We're near peace." It reads: "Talks with Croats progressing. If so, we are near peace."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the next page, it's R0164043, it would be the third page of your diary entry, since two pages are reflected in each ERN range, it indicates at the top of the page, again next to an asterisk: "Main problem, Tito's borders. But if Serbs and Croats `are clever', exchange borders voluntarily, this exchange would help." Can you tell us what those remarks refer to, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they refer to was the cooperation, sometimes overt, sometimes covert, between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats. This cooperation was at the expense of the Bosnian Muslims and occurred because in some respects, but not all respects, but in some respects Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat objectives were congruent in Bosnia. Each, for example, had declared its own political entity. Republika Srpska by the Bosnian Serbs; Herceg Bosna by the Bosnian Croats. Each wanted to be ruled only under their own governance. Each wanted it ethnically cleansed and pure, which I should note was easier for the Bosnian Croats in Herceg Bosna, that is to say, in Herzegovina because Herzegovina was already 98 per cent or so ethnic Croat. And the problem for the Bosnian Croats was Central Bosnia where the population was a mixed one as between Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat. But the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats each wished to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, to carve out of the body of Bosnia and Herzegovina their own separate mini state. So there was a congruence of views. Now, it also happens that they were fighting each other at the same time because there were areas that were in contest between the Serbs and the Croats. The Neretva valley, for example. The Bosnian Serbs wanted the Neretva valley. You'll recall it's one of the points in their May 12, 1992, strategic objectives. They speak of it. Well, the Bosnian Croats were not about to give them the Neretva valley, first, because it's important economically; second, because what the Bosnian Croats consider their capital, Mostar, is on the Neretva. It should be noted that Mostar is still divided to this day as between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. It is still divided by the river, 2004. So you can see that it meant a great deal to the Croats. Just as the Bosnian Serbs had and held and regarded Banja Luka as their capital, so, too, the Bosnian Croats held and regarded Mostar as their capital. So there were, in certain areas, cooperation, collaboration, congruence as between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats. But they also were fighting each other for areas where they didn't agree, and the Bosnian Croat Army was large because it was being assisted by the regular Croatian Army which had come in to Bosnia early in the conflict. It crossed over the Sava at Bosanski Brod. So the Bosnian Croats were well armed and well led. And Dr. Karadzic knew that and said that to us very, very frequently. And that was the situation. That's why he says, "We're talking, we're making progress with the Bosnian Croats. If we decide things between us, there can be peace." Well, you notice he never mentions the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, if I could ask you to look at a map, which is marked 03574817.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me ask you if you're familiar with that map, and if you could explain to us whether or not that bears on your explanation about the interest in collaboration between the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I'm familiar with the map. Anybody who deals with Yugoslavia must be familiar with this map. It is the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement of 1939, the agreement between a leading Serb and a leading Croat to divide what was then called the Banovina. The king had changed the name to banovinas. The banovina of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's the partition, the carve-up of Bosnia between the Serbs and the Croats. And it was decided upon in the spring, I believe it was, of 1939 and would have happened except that World War II intervened and Nazi Germany took precedence everywhere in Europe.
